newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire envoy backs away from idea of peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire envoy backs away from idea of peace talks.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew and chief security adviser backed away from the idea of peace talks in South Africa with Zaire's rebel foes under an initiative announced by President Nelson Mandela.
But a South African source told Reuters that representatives from the two sides remained in Cape Town and implied that a meeting was still possible.
A senior South African official said earlier that both sides were very reluctant to acknowledge they were willing to talk.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said in New York that face-to- face talks would be difficult and so-called proximity talks -- separate conversations with each delegation by mediators -- might have to take place first.
But Mobutu's nephew Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba told Radio France International by telephone from Cape Town that Zaire had pre-conditions for any talks and there would be no meeting in South Africa.
"There's never been any question of meeting any member of the (Zairean) rebellion in South Africa," he said.

"For us there are conditions. We want first of all the real people behind this aggression to show their goodwill and respect the decisions of the Security Council," he added, referring for a U.N. call for all foreign forces to withdraw.

Zaire says forces from Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi invaded its territory in support of Tutsi-led rebels who took up arms in October accusing Zaire of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them.

"We are being attacked by three neighbouring countries and we demand that the three neighbouring countries pull out their soldiers and let Zaireans find a solution to their internal problems," Ngbanda said.

He was speaking after a day of confusion in Cape Town reinforced suspicions that Mandela jumped the gun by going public on Wednesday on plans for a meeting, which various sources indicated was to have taken place in secrecy.
South Africa later put a lid on all news of the peace initiative and diplomats suggested that Mandela's breach of confidentiality might have set things back.
Mandela said both rebel leader Laurent Kabila and Mobutu had asked to meet in South Africa. A diplomatic source said the first approach had in fact come from Mobutu's side.
A South African source, asked late on Thursday if the initiative had been derailed, replied simply: "They are still here."
In Washington, State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said the United States was ready to lend diplomatic support to South Africa's mediation efforts.

He said Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs George Moose and National Security Council official Susan Rice were both in Cape Town and were "willing and able to help to the extent that they're called upon to help."

Zaire's government said earlier it would resume air raids on rebel positions in the east and told civilians to leave the war zone. Relief officials said at least 19 people were killed in air raids on Monday.
The Zairean government launched a counter-offensive on January 20 but the rebels hit back on several fronts and blunted its impact.
